senses: Of a bristle, having split, bushy ends.
Of a swab, having dense fibers with a desirable nap to optimize collection and elution of specimens.
Of a Christmas tree, covered with artificial snow.
ety: From flock (“tufts of wool, lock of hair”).

senses: Having a smooth circular cross-section; cylindrical, commonly more or less tapering.
Any of a family of fragrances built on a base consisting of bergamot, oakmoss and labdanum.
ety: French Chypre (“Cyprus”), the name of a perfume created by François Coty in 1917.

senses: Something having a certain number of suits.
Something that can hold a certain number of suits.
examples: Additionally your chances of going alone and getting all five tricks are rather better on a two-suited hand than a one-suiter.
He lifted the big three-suiter onto the bed and opened it.

senses: A red flag used by bullfighters.
ety: Borrowed from Spanish muleta, diminutive of mula (“mule”).
examples: Out in the center of the ring Romero profiled in front of the bull, drew the sword out from the folds of the muleta, rose on his toes, and sighted along the blade.

senses: An aircraft that uses such an engine.
Plump; fat; sleek.
An ordinary citizen.
The narrow side of chimney stack, a haunch.
The side of an arch from the topmost part (crown) to the bottommost part (impost).
A limp; lameness.
A dog of a certain breed, similar to a small greyhound, originating in Britain and bred for racing.
On fire (often metaphorically).
ety: 13ᵗʰc., from Middle English afire, equivalent to a- (“on”) + fire. Figurative usage from late 14ᵗʰc.

senses: Having (a specified form of) fibres.
examples: The center of a peach ripe, soft, pitted, red-fibred flesh

senses: A small rod, usually made of wood, pressed against the melody course of a lap dulcimer to change the pitches.
An optical device for viewing extremely small objects.
The territory governed by a ban.
ety: Equivalent to ban (“a warden”) + -ate. Compare French banat, German Banat.

senses: Any one of a series of small rectangular blocks projecting like teeth from a molding or beneath a cornice.
ety: From French dentille, ultimately from Latin dente, ablative singular of dēns.

senses: An atom of this element.
ety: From Ancient Greek κρυπτός (kruptós, “hidden”) + -on, used for all noble gases.

senses: A small-scale symphony (either in length or size of orchestra needed).
A small orchestra.
ety: Either: * from Italian sinfonietta; * formed on the Italian roots sinfonia (“symphony”) + -etta (feminine diminutive suffix), either in English or in German (as Sinfonietta) and adopted thence; or, * an alteration of the French symphoniette to resemble an Italian construction of the form sinfonia + -etta. Compare the French–Italian hybrid symphonietta.

senses: A narrow border near the edge of a shield or banner.
ety: From Middle English tressour, from a mixture of Old French tressure and tresseor. By surface analysis, tress + -ure.

senses: Plasterwork imitating marble, granite, etc.
ety: Borrowed from Italian scagliola, a diminutive of scaglia.

senses: railway tracks collectively
The right of a railway company to use the tracks belonging to another; the charge levied for this right
The act of tracking, or towing, as a boat; towage.
A mate; a kinsman.
ety: From Warlpiri [Term?], and other related languages of the Northern Territory and northern Queensland.

senses: Synonym of continuer, a person who continues the work of another.
examples: The History of the Patriarchs of Alexandria is traditionally ascribed to the 10th-century Severus of Hermopolis, but it contains appendices by various continuators that carry its narrative into the 19th century.
Ms. Sheinbaum, who lacks his charisma and political acumen, is seen as the continuator of his political project.

senses: Farsighted; of, having, or pertaining to hyperopia.
A passive device that implements frequency domain multiplexing.
The act of ovulation through, or by means of, one's anus.
The edible root of the yam bean (Pachyrhizus erosus) used in salads in Central America and as a snack in Mexico.
ety: Borrowed from Mexican Spanish jícama, from Classical Nahuatl xīcama, apocopic form of xīcamatl.

senses: A male worker in a mill.
A Portuguese gentleman.
ety: From Portuguese senhor, which see for more. Doublet of seigneur, seignior, senior, señor, senyor, signore, sir, and sire.

senses: A demon or witch in French folklore that drains a sleeping person's energy by night.
Synonym of orcharder.
That has both optical and electronic components, especially such components that interact.
The organ a spider uses to spin its web.
A multipored device through which a plastic polymer melt is extruded into fibers.
A cloud with a tall structure and flat base, often associated with thunderstorms.
The outer, protective layer of the skin of vertebrates.
The similar outer layer of cells in invertebrates and plants.
ety: Borrowed from Latin epidermis, from Ancient Greek ἐπιδερμίς (epidermís), ἐπί (epí, “on top of”) + δέρμα (dérma, “skin”). Equivalent to epi- + dermis.

senses: The quality or state of being tolerable.
Any substance added to something in order to stabilize it, as for example a fuel additive that prolongs the shelf life of petrol.
An additional wheel on a bicycle to keep it upright to assist a learner.
A gyroscopically controlled fin or similar device that prevents the excess rolling of a ship in rough seas.
An airfoil that stabilizes the flight of an aircraft or missile.
A piece of backing fabric used in embroidery.
cycle path, cycle lane
examples: Part of the old line (which closed in 1972) is today a cycleway from Keswick to Threlkeld.

senses: Shield-shaped; scutiform.
ety: From Ancient Greek πέλτη (péltē) + English -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

senses: Measured in cubits.
Of the length of a cubit.
